w: Built over the tomb of Saint Benignus between 1280 and 1325, this Gothic pile only became a cathedral during the French Revolution, when the old one down the road was secularised. It has been the Archbishop of Dijon's seat since 2002 - a promotion six centuries in the waiting.
s: Gothic seat raised over a Burgundian saint's tomb
_facts: Built 1280-1325 over the tomb of Saint Benignus of Dijon, dedicated 1393
Became a cathedral during the French Revolution when the previous one was secularised
Seat of the Archbishopric of Dijon since its elevation in 2002

w: Founded in 1832 and housed since 1934 in the old wing of the Abbey of St Benigne, right next door to Dijon Cathedral, this museum tracks what it calls 'the men of Burgundy' from prehistory through Roman rule to the Middle Ages, with paleochristian and sacred art thrown in.
s: Burgundy's prehistory to Middle Ages, beside the cathedral
_facts: Founded 1832, focused on Burgundy archaeology
Housed since 1934 in the main wing of the Abbey of St Benigne, next to Dijon Cathedral
Covers prehistory, protohistory, Roman rule and the Middle Ages, plus paleochristian and sacred art

w: Grown out of the association Le Coin du Miroir, this contemporary art centre began life in a 600 square metre former appliance store in downtown Dijon before outgrowing it for a 4,000 square metre factory on the city's edge. In 2011 it moved again, into a new building designed by Shigeru Ban.
s: Contemporary art empire born in an old appliance store
_facts: Founded by Xavier Douroux and Franck Gautherot from the association Le Coin du Miroir
Moved from a 600sqm former appliance store to a 4,000sqm ex-factory in 1991, then a Shigeru Ban-designed building in 2011
Awarded the Art Center label in 1982; runs a London office on Hoxton Street since 2009

w: Chevaliers of the arquebus once trained on this ground before their captain turned part of it into an English garden in the late 1700s. Free and open daily since becoming city property in 1803, it holds close to 4,000 plant species, a 100,000-specimen herbarium, and a flock of wild ducks, geese and swans.
s: Free botanical garden on an old chevaliers' drill ground
_facts: Former 16th-century training ground for chevaliers of the arquebus
English garden added late 18th century, became city property 1803; first botanical garden's plants moved here 1833
Nearly 4,000 plant species today, 100,000-specimen herbarium, collection of Anatidae (wild ducks, geese, swans)

w: Running from Place Darcy to Place de la Liberation, this pedestrian shopping street is lined almost entirely with buildings dating from the 15th to the 18th centuries, all classified as monuments historiques. Walk it for the shops and you're browsing inside a protected slice of ducal Dijon.
s: Dijon's grand pedestrian spine, buildings the age of dukes
_facts: Main street of historic-centre Dijon, connecting Place Darcy to Place de la Liberation
Pedestrian shopping street lined with buildings from the 15th-18th centuries
Buildings classified as monuments historiques

w: Housed since 1947 in part of Dijon's 11th-century Eglise Saint-Etienne, this free museum displays life-size plaster casts by sculptor Francois Rude, bought up by the city between 1887 and 1910. Below sits an archaeological crypt and the old Roman-era gate the church was built over.
s: A sculptor's plaster casts inside an 11th-century church
_facts: Dedicated to sculptor Francois Rude (1784-1855), housed since 1947 in the former Eglise Saint-Etienne
Displays life-size plaster casts acquired by Dijon between 1887 and 1910; originals held in museums including the Louvre
Museum also shows an 11th-century archaeological crypt and the former 3rd-century St Etienne Gate of the Dijon castrum

w: Inaugurated in 1980 inside the former Eglise Sainte-Anne, bought by the city in 1950 for exactly this purpose, the museum gathers what the Church set aside through generations of reform: sculpture, vestments, relics and liturgical objects spanning the 12th to 19th centuries, plus works by Jean-Baptiste Bouchardon.
s: Catholic Burgundy's robes, relics and liturgical treasures
_facts: Municipal museum of Catholic Burgundian sacred art, inaugurated 1980 in the former Eglise Sainte-Anne at 17 rue Sainte-Anne
City bought the church in 1950 to house the museum
Exhibits liturgical objects and vestments from the 12th-19th centuries, and works by Jean-Baptiste Bouchardon

w: Carved between 1395 and 1403 by Dutch sculptor Claus Sluter for the Chartreuse de Champmol, the monastery Duke Philip the Bold built as his own burial site, this sculpture was meant to anchor a Calvary scene above six Old Testament prophets. Only the base survives, and it's still ranked as Sluter's masterpiece.
s: Sluter's stone prophets, carved for a duke's burial ground
_facts: Monumental sculpture by Dutch sculptor Claus Sluter (assisted by nephew Claus de Werve), carved 1395-1403
Built for the Carthusian monastery of Chartreuse de Champmol, Duke Philip the Bold's burial site, just outside Dijon
Recognised as Sluter's masterpiece

w: Maurice Magnin and his sister Jeanne spent decades amassing some 2,000 artworks, then bequeathed the whole collection to the State in 1938 along with the house built to hold it: the Hotel Lantin, a 17th-century townhouse in old Dijon, kept exactly as an amateur collector's family home.
s: A collector's cabinet of curiosities in a 17th-century house
_facts: National museum with around 2,000 works collected by Maurice and Jeanne Magnin, bequeathed to the State in 1938
Displayed in the Hotel Lantin, a 17th-century hotel particulier in Dijon's old-town quarter
Presented as an amateur collector's cabinet of curiosities and family home
